p65: 65.  In the context of Article 10, the Contracting States have a certain margin of appreciation in assessing whether an interference with the exercise of the right to freedom of expression is “necessary in a democratic society”. This margin of appreciation, however, goes hand in hand with European supervision, embracing both the legislation and the decisions applying it, even those given by an independent court (see Tammer v. Estonia, no. 41205/98, § 60, ECHR 2001-I, Peck v. the United Kingdom, no. 44647/98, § 77, ECHR 2003-I, and Karhuvaara and Iltalehti v. Finland, no. 53678/00, § 38, ECHR 2004-X). In exercising its supervisory function, the Court’s task is not to take the place of the national courts, but rather to review, in the light of the case as a whole, the decisions they have taken pursuant to their power of appreciation (see Petrenco v. Moldova, no. 20928/05, § 54, 30 March 2010, Polanco Torres and Movilla Polanco v. Spain, no. 34147/06, § 41, 21 September 2010, and Petrov v. Bulgaria (dec.), no. 27103/04, 2 November 2010).
p66: 66.  Thus, in similar cases, the Court has attached considerable weight to the fact that the domestic authorities had established the existence of conflicting rights and the need to strike a fair balance between them (see, for example and mutatis mutandis, Tammer, cited above, § 69; White v. Sweden, no. 42435/02, § 27, 19 September 2006, Standard Verlags GmbH v. Austria (no. 2), no. 21277/05, § 52, 4 June 2009, Lappalainen v. Finland (dec.), no. 22175/06, 20 January 2009, and Papaianopol v. Romania, no. 17590/02, § 30, 16 March 2010).
p67: 67.  If the balance struck by the national judicial authorities is unsatisfactory, in particular because the importance or the scope of one of the fundamental rights at stake was not duly considered, the margin of appreciation accorded to the decisions of the national courts will be a narrow one. However, where the balancing exercise has been undertaken in conformity with the criteria laid down in the Court’s well-established case-law, the Court would require strong reasons to substitute its view for that of the domestic courts, to which a wide margin of appreciation is accordingly granted (see MGN Limited v. the United Kingdom, no. 39401/04, §§ 150-155, 18 January 2011, and Von Hannover v. Germany (no. 2) [GC], nos. 40660/08 and 60641/08, § 107, ECHR 2012).
p68: 68.  All of this presupposes that an effective legal system for the protection of the rights falling within the notion of “private life” was in place and was available to the applicant (see Karakó v. Hungary, no. 39311/05, § 19, 28 April 2009). The Court must therefore also examine that issue.
p69: 69.  In the present case, the domestic courts were required to strike a fair balance between, on the one hand, the applicant’s rights under Article 8 of the Convention as a member of the Roma community and, on the other, the freedom of the author of the impugned book to carry out academic/scientific research on a specific ethnic group and to publish his findings. According to the applicant, the book, and in particular the chapter dealing with the living conditions of Roma in various Turkish cities, constituted an insult to the Roma community. The Turkish courts dismissed that complaint at two successive levels of jurisdiction, relying in particular on a report prepared by seven university professors which had concluded that the impugned book was an academic study based on scientific research (see paragraph 25 above). They held that the impugned remarks and expressions were not insulting, that they were of a general nature, that they did not target all Roma and that they did not amount to an attack on the applicant’s identity (see paragraphs 21 and 23 above). Furthermore, the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance (*tribunal de grande instance d’Ankara*) found that the book dealt with the social structures of Roma/Gypsies in Turkey and was based on scientific data (see paragraph 21 above).
